cues.text: Every job comes with a plan, written earlier, somewhere else.
But the job is here, now. It may not match the plan.
The 2-minute rule is how you catch the difference.
It's a short, deliberate pause you take where you do the work.
Take it right before you start, and again after a break, a handover, or any change.
It adds to your SOPs, permits, lockout, and confined-space programs. It never replaces them.
Two minutes is a rule of thumb. What matters is the pause.
It's not the productivity tip about doing quick tasks right away.
You already do this for product. It's called line clearance.
Right before use, you inspect the packaging line so nothing from the last run remains.
21 CFR 211.130(e) requires it, and the results go in the batch record.
The 2-minute rule is line clearance for people.
Same discipline, aimed at the hazards around you.
In your two minutes: stop, look, ask, decide.
Stop before you touch anything. Look around the job, and next to it.
Then ask: What's different from the plan, or last time? What could hurt us?
Are the controls checked, or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
Then decide: go, fix it if it's safe, or stop and get help.
What's different? First run after a tooling change on the tablet press.
What could hurt us? Clean- or steam-in-place: hot caustic and steam.
Checked or assumed? The blister packer is locked out. Did you verify it yourself?
What if it goes wrong while you're charging a reactor? What's your next move?
Rushed, tired, or distracted? Check yourself, too.
A real case: a biopharmaceutical plant in Los Angeles, January 2011.
Nitrogen bubbles through plasma in a 6,000-liter tank, as part of the process.
The nitrogen has pushed out the oxygen, and the air is untested.
A technician goes in to take a temperature reading. He collapses.
Two coworkers go in to bring him out, with no air test and no proper rescue gear provided.
Both of them collapse too.
Firefighters bring them out. The technician dies.
This isn't about careless people. It's about the gaps around them.
At two moments, a pause could have changed the outcome. First, before entry.
What's different? Nitrogen is still flowing in, and it isn't isolated.
What could hurt us? The air: nitrogen has no color and no smell.
Oxygen-poor air can knock you out in one or two breaths.
Checked or assumed? Has anyone measured the oxygen? Does entry need a permit?
The only way to know is to isolate and test.
Can I take the reading from outside instead?
What if it goes wrong? Who's watching me, and what's the rescue plan?
No test, no plan: stop and get help.
Second: someone is down inside a vessel.
Wanting to rush in is human. Run the questions anyway, even in seconds.
What could hurt us? Assume the air did this.
What if it goes wrong? More people go down.
Don't go in. Call trained rescue, keep others out, use retrieval gear.
That only works if the plan and gear exist beforehand.
Cal/OSHA issued 11 citations, four of them willful.
It found the employer didn't test the tank's air.
The employer's confined-space program fell short on air testing, protective gear, and rescue.
Those findings are about the employer's program, not about the technician.
There's a design lesson, too: a reading shouldn't require going inside.
An installed probe or a sample port means no one has to.
A pause can't supply a gas meter, a permit system, or a rescue team.
The rule works when the organization gives you tools, time, and authority to stop.
That means stopping with no reprisal.
Leaders who thank you, then fix what you found.
Near-miss reports that lead to learning, not discipline.
And hazards engineered out, so the pause isn't your only defense.
One 2022 study of Take 5 pre-task cards found no evidence the cards made work safer.
So the pause is a professional habit, and a gateway to stopping.
Not a check-the-box form, and never a tool for blame.
Before you start, and whenever things change: stop, look, and ask.
What's different? What could hurt us?
Are the controls checked, or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
Then go, fix it if it's safe, or stop and get help.
You know this work best.
You clear the line for product. Clear it for people, too.
